The feast was laid in a water-pavilion. Lotus ponds ringed it on every side, washed to a clean and single green, and only the balustrade of the nine-turn zigzag bridge ran a bright vermilion. The pearl-gauze windows stood propped high, and the breeze came in scented with the year's first lotus leaves. It was April now.

Hua Manlou sat quietly, taking in that spaciousness and fragrance which belong only to a house of great wealth. He could not, of course, see what Huo Tianqing looked like; but from the man's voice he had already gauged what kind of man he was. Huo Tianqing's voice was low and strong, and he spoke slowly and mildly, in a way that wished every ear turned to him and every word of his heard clearly. It was the voice of a man sure of himself and sound in his judgment, who had his own rule for whatever he did: a proud man, who would rather others did not think him proud. Hua Manlou did not dislike him, and Huo Tianqing, for his part, did not dislike Hua Manlou.

There were two other guests to keep the table company. One was the Yan household's resident tutor and man of letters, Su Shaoqing; the other was Ma Xingkong, chief armsman of the Allied Escort Houses of Guanzhong, known in the martial world as the Divine Dragon in the Clouds. Ma Xingkong's name had stood high a long while, and the skill in his hands was real, no hollow reputation; but what Hua Manlou found strange was that whenever the man spoke to Huo Tianqing there was an unaccountable note of fawning in his voice, a flattery past explaining. A hero who had won his place in the world by his own two hands had no business wearing such an air.

Su Shaoqing, by contrast, was an easy, unaffected man, with neither the sour breath of the pedant nor the trick of taking the mawkish for the droll. Huo Tianqing had made a point of introducing him as a learned juren, a graduate of the provincial examinations; yet by his voice he seemed very young.
Host and guests together came to only five, which was the very way Hua Manlou best liked to be entertained: it showed a host not merely attentive but nice in his reading of a guest's heart.
And yet the wine and dishes had still not been brought; and though Hua Manlou was in no hurry, he could not help finding it a little strange.
The lamps in the pavilion were few, yet it was bright as broad day, for bright pearls hung on all four walls; the lamplight met the pearl-light, and the soft glow of it gave a comfort past words.

Su Shaoqing was in flowing, easy talk just then, telling over the romantic doings of the Last Ruler of the Southern Tang. "They say that in the bedchamber he shared with the younger Empress Zhou, no lamp was ever lit. The story-books have it so. A great general of Jiangnan, having taken one of the Emperor Li's favourite concubines, showed her a lamp one night; she shut her eyes and said, 'The smoke.' He changed it for wax candles; she shut her eyes again and said, 'The smoke is worse.' Someone asked her: were no lamps or candles ever burned in the palace, then? And she answered: in the water-pavilions of the palace, at every nightfall they hung out great treasure-pearls, and the light of them filled the room, bright as noon."
Huo Tianqing smiled. "The Last Ruler's extravagance went past all bounds. The fall of the Southern Tang was only ever a question of time."
"A man of too much feeling," said Su Shaoqing lightly, "isn't fit to be an emperor in the first place."
Ma Xingkong laughed. "But had he a man like Steward Huo for his chancellor, perhaps the Southern Tang need never have fallen at all."
Lu Xiaofeng let out a sudden sigh. "It seems the only pity is that Li Yu was born a few hundred years too soon. Were he here today, he'd be even hungrier to get at the wine than I am."
Hua Manlou laughed.

Huo Tianqing could not help a laugh of his own. "The food and wine are in fact all ready. The pity's that when the Boss heard he'd have guests today like Lu Xiaofeng and young Master Hua, he was set on coming to join the fun himself."
"We're waiting for him, then?" said Lu Xiaofeng.
"If the wait wears on you," said Huo Tianqing, "we might set out a few plain dishes and start without him."
Ma Xingkong cut in at once. "A little longer won't do any harm. The Boss is rarely in so fine a humour as today; how could we spoil his pleasure?"
From beyond the pavilion a voice broke in, laughing. "And I'd not spoil yours either, gentlemen. Come, the wine, the wine, and be quick about it!"
A man came in on a gale of laughter, a laugh high and thin. His face was white and plump, the skin fine as a maiden's; only a great hooked nose, like an eagle's beak, lent it any cast of manhood.
Hua Manlou thought to himself: this man was once keeper of the inner treasury of the Great King of the Golden Roc. Could he be a eunuch?
Ma Xingkong was already on his feet, smiling ingratiatingly. "Boss! A good evening to you!"

Yan Tieshan did not spare him so much as a glance. He caught Lu Xiaofeng by the hand instead, looked him up and down, and burst out laughing. "The same as ever; not a hair changed since the day I saw you on the Sunwatch Peak of Mount Tai. Only, how is it your eyebrows are down to two?"
He never for a moment let the Shanxi twang out of his speech, as though his one fear were that a man might take him for anything but Shanxi-born and Shanxi-bred.
Lu Xiaofeng's eyes glinted, and he smiled. "I drank without the money to pay, so the wine-shop's landlady scraped off even my whiskers to make herself a powder-brush."
Yan Tieshan roared. "His granny's, that hot little baggage must have liked the feel of your whiskers on her face."

He turned then and clapped Hua Manlou on the shoulder. "And you'll be the seventh of the Hua boys, I'll be bound. Several of your brothers have been to me here in their time; the third and the fifth could both hold their drink uncommon well."
Hua Manlou smiled. "The seventh can manage a cup or two himself."
Yan Tieshan clapped his hands. "Good, excellent! Fetch out those jars of old Fen wine I've got hid under my bed. Any man who stays sober tonight is his granny's little brother-in-law!"

Shanxi Fen wine is of course best aged, and the dishes were fine as well. The live carp alone, done three ways, one portion crisp-fried, one red-braised, and one served soft in a thick broth, was enough to set a man feasting in earnest.

With a pair of soft white hands Yan Tieshan kept heaping Lu Xiaofeng's bowl. "This is our Shanxi speciality. Nothing very grand, mind; but his granny's, you'll not taste the like of it anywhere else."
"Your old home's Shanxi, then, Boss?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

Yan Tieshan laughed. "Born and bred a country clod, that's me. In all these decades I've been out of it just the once, up Mount Tai, to watch his granny's famous sunrise. And I looked and I looked, and all I saw was one great egg-yolk. No sense in it at all."
His granny's this and his granny's that, at every breath, as though he were bent on proving to the company that here was a big, rough, plain-spoken man and nothing more.
Lu Xiaofeng laughed too. He raised his cup, smiling, and said all at once, "And Steward Yan, where might he hail from, I wonder?"
Ma Xingkong put in quickly, "Steward Huo, you mean. Not Steward Yan."

"It wasn't the Steward Huo of the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour I meant," said Lu Xiaofeng evenly. "I meant Yan Liben, keeper of the inner treasury, in the old days, of the dynasty of the Golden Roc."
He fixed his eyes on Yan Tieshan without a blink, and went on, word by measured word, "A man the Boss is surely acquainted with."
Yan Tieshan's smooth, soft, white face drew tight of a sudden as a bowstring, and the smile on it turned strange and stiff.

He was, in the common way, a man who let neither joy nor anger show; but Lu Xiaofeng's words were a whip, and one stroke of them had split open a scar decades old, so that the mortal wound beneath began to bleed again.

A light had kindled in Lu Xiaofeng's eyes. He went on, slowly, "If the Boss is acquainted with the man, he might pass a word to him. Tell him there's an old account, decades old, that someone's now ready to settle."
Yan Tieshan's face was rigid. "Steward Huo," he said abruptly.
Huo Tianqing, unmoved in voice or face, answered, "Here."
"Young Master Hua and young Master Lu no longer care to linger here," said Yan Tieshan coldly. "Go and make ready a carriage for them. They will be leaving at once."
Before the words were well out he had risen with a sweep of his sleeve and was striding for the door, not once looking back.
But he had not yet cleared the doorway when a man appeared beyond it and barred his way. "They are not ready to leave," the man said coldly. "And you had far better stay where you are."
He stood tall and straight, his robe white as snow; but the sword at his waist was black, lacquer-black, long and narrow, and old.
Yan Tieshan's eyes flew wide. "Who dares such insolence?" he demanded harshly.
"Ximen Chuixue!"
Ximen Chuixue. The name itself was like the edge of a sword: cold, and keen.
Yan Tieshan, in spite of himself, gave back two steps; then all at once he bellowed, "Guards! To me!"
Apart from two young pages waiting at the side to pour the wine, and the blue-clad house-servants who came and went with the dishes, the pavilion within and without lay silent; not a shadow stirred.

But at the Boss's shout, five men came flying in over the sill on the instant, their weapons flashing: a Wu-hook sword, a goose-quill saber, a chain-whip spear, a pair of chicken-claw sickles, a three-section steel staff.
Five weapons, every one cunningly wrought, and all of the outer, uncommon kind; men who could wield such arms were past doubt masters of the martial world.
Ximen Chuixue did not spare them a glance. "Once my sword leaves the sheath," he said coldly, "it takes a life. Will you truly force me to draw it?"
Three of the five had gone green in the face already; but men who do not fear death are to be found everywhere.
There came a swift hiss of wind, and the goose-quill saber whirled up a flowering blur of steel, hacking seven strokes in a breath at Ximen Chuixue.
The three-section staff turned in the same instant to a low wind sweeping the ground, lashing across at Ximen Chuixue's knees.
The one weapon all fierce force, the other all quickness; the strokes were keen, and the two men worked well together. Plainly they had trained side by side a long time.
Ximen Chuixue's pupils contracted sharply; and in that one instant his sword was out of its sheath.
Huo Tianqing did not move. He only watched Lu Xiaofeng, quietly; and while Lu Xiaofeng did not move, neither by any means would he.
But Ma Xingkong had shot to his feet. "Steward Huo asks you here in good faith to drink his wine," he cried, "and it turns out you've come to make trouble!"

On the shout his hand went to his waist and came up with a fish-scaled coiling-dragon rod of purple gold; he snapped it out to its full length against the wind and drove it straight for Hua Manlou's throat.
He had marked Hua Manlou for a blind man, and reckoned a blind man the easier to bully.
But there was, in truth, an uncommon trick to that coiling-dragon rod. As the thrust drove home there came a click, and out of the dragon's mouth sprang a short blade, thin and keen.
Hua Manlou sat still, and waited; then two fingers shot out and closed, another click, and the dragon's-tongue blade, for all its hundred-times-tempered steel, broke in three.
Ma Xingkong's face changed. With a shake of his wrist the rod spun back and struck in reverse, its two dragon's-horns stabbing for the base of Hua Manlou's skull behind the left ear.
Hua Manlou sighed. His sleeve swept out like a flying cloud, wrapped the rod, and drew it lightly aside.

And Ma Xingkong pitched forward across the table, smashing a wide swath of bowls and dishes; Hua Manlou gave another gentle push, and the man flew up and out through the window and came down in the lotus pond with a great splash.
"Fine skill!" Su Shaoqing exclaimed, before he could help it.
"Not my skill," said Hua Manlou mildly. "His has fallen off. The Divine Dragon in the Clouds keeps at the most half the art he had in his prime. Can he have taken some grave inner wound?"
"A shrewd eye," said Su Shaoqing. "Three years ago he did indeed take an air-splitting palm-stroke from Steward Huo."
"That'd explain it," said Hua Manlou.

Now at last he understood why Ma Xingkong was so fawning a creature. A man who lives by licking blood from the blade, once he has lost the better half of his skill, must find himself a wall to lean on; and where would he find a stouter wall than the Pavilion of Pearls and Splendour?
Su Shaoqing said suddenly, "I'd like to try young Master Hua's art too: the reading of a place by its sounds, the flying-cloud sleeve. If you please!"
The word was barely spoken when the chopsticks in his hand thrust out on a slant.
This gentle, scholarly youth, with a pair of ivory chopsticks for a sword, was suddenly plying an orthodox inner-school swordplay; in the blink of an eye he had dealt Hua Manlou seven thrusts.
Lu Xiaofeng did not move. He only watched Huo Tianqing, quietly; and while Huo Tianqing did not move, neither by any means would he.

Three men lay on the floor already who would never move again. The goose-quill saber stood slanted in the window-lattice; the three-section staff had flown out of doors; the chain-whip spear had snapped in four.
When the sword came back out, there was blood on its point.
Ximen Chuixue blew on it, lightly, and the fresh blood ran off the point in a string of drops.
His face was empty as ever, but the cold eyes had lit; and he looked coldly at Yan Tieshan, and said coldly, "You should have raised your own hand. Why send other men to their deaths?"
Yan Tieshan sneered. "Because I bought their lives long ago."
He waved a hand, and six or seven more men appeared within the pavilion and without; while his own eyes flickered here and there, already seeking a way out.
There was no Shanxi twang in his speech now, and no more cursing; but his voice had grown shriller and finer, every word of it a needle-point pricking at the ear.
Lu Xiaofeng gave a sudden little smile. "So the Boss is himself a master of deep inner force."
Huo Tianqing smiled a little too. "I doubt there's a man in this room to match him," he said mildly.
"A pity that however high his skill, it won't serve him," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Why so?" said Huo Tianqing.
"Because he's got one mortal weakness," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"What weakness?" said Huo Tianqing.
"He's afraid to die," said Lu Xiaofeng.

Su Shaoqing had loosed his second round of seven linked thrusts, the sword-light quick and light, the changes strange and clever, every stroke playing about the inch of ground at Hua Manlou's ear and eye.
Hua Manlou still sat where he was. He had taken up an ivory chopstick of his own, and at the least motion of it Su Shaoqing's fierce onset was turned aside as lightly as a line drawn in dust.

Su Shaoqing's second seven thrusts ended abruptly, his hand staying itself. He had suddenly seen that this ever-smiling blind man seemed to understand the swordplay he used better than he understood it himself.
Each thrust he made, the other seemed to know his next before he made it. He could not keep from asking, "Are you too of the Emei line? Do you know the Emei swordplay?"
Hua Manlou shook his head, smiling. "To you there are many sword-schools, and the strokes of each are different. But to a blind man, every swordplay in the world is one and the same."
It was one of the deepest truths of the martial art. Su Shaoqing half grasped it and half did not; he wished to ask, and did not so much as know how the question should be framed.
But Hua Manlou was already asking him, "Can you be one of the Seven Swords of Emei?"
Su Shaoqing hesitated, and said at last, "I am Su Shaoying."
Hua Manlou smiled. "Su the Second, then, of the Three Heroes and Four Beauties."
Then Ximen Chuixue said coldly, "If this man is a student of the sword as well, why has he not come to me?"
Su Shaoying's face went suddenly white; there was a click, and the ivory chopstick snapped in his own hand.
Ximen Chuixue sneered. "They say the Emei swordplay stands alone in all of Shu. Can it be no more than an empty name?"
Su Shaoying set his teeth and spun about, in time to see the last drop of fresh blood fall from the point of Ximen Chuixue's sword.
Lu Xiaofeng and Huo Tianqing still sat gazing at each other, quietly, each as though waiting for the other to move first.

Seven men lay on the floor now who would never move again, and not one of the seven but had been a master of the first rank; yet each in a single instant had had his throat run through by Ximen Chuixue's sword.
The muscles at the corners of Yan Tieshan's eyes had begun to twitch; and only now could a man see that he was in truth an old one.
Yet for these men who had spent their lives at his bidding he felt not a particle of grief or pity.
He had not fled, only because the sure moment had not yet come, and the hour of no choice was not yet upon him.
The four men still able to fight had lost the stomach for it; at the sight of Su Shaoying coming forward they gave way at once and cleared him a path.
Su Shaoying's step was steady still; only there was no colour at all left in his white face.
Ximen Chuixue watched him coldly. "What sword do you use?" he said coldly.
Su Shaoying sneered in his turn. "Any sword that can kill, I can use."
"Good," said Ximen Chuixue. "There are swords on the floor. Choose one."
Two swords lay on the floor, in the pools of blood.
One was narrow and long and keen; the other broad and thick and heavy.
Su Shaoying hesitated a moment, then flicked up a toe; a sword sprang from the ground into the air and fell into his hand.
The Emei swordplay is prized above all for lightness and change, yet the blade he had chosen was the heavier one.
The youth meant to set the strength of young arms, and a heavy, driving, violent swordplay, against the honed and cutting line of Ximen Chuixue's blade.
The choice was in itself a sound one: every disciple trained under Dugu Yihe was schooled to good judgment.
But this once he was wrong. He should never have lifted any sword at all.
Ximen Chuixue gazed at him. "In another twenty years," he said suddenly, "your swordplay might come to something."
"Oh?" said Su Shaoying.
"And so I have no wish to kill you now," said Ximen Chuixue. "Come and find me again in twenty years."
"Twenty years is too long," Su Shaoying cried out suddenly. "I can't wait so long!"

He was a young man after all, with the hot blood high in him; a surge of it rose in his breast, and the sword in his hand struck out in linked blows, with something in the swordplay of the broad, sweeping violence of the saber.

This was Dugu Yihe's own creation, the Saber-and-Sword Double Kill, seven times seven, the forty-nine forms. He had come to the Emei gate already deep-versed in the saber; and over thirty hard years he had worked the saber's fierce, driving weight into the clear and elegant swordplay of Emei.
These forty-nine forms of his own devising could be plied with saber or with sword alike: a skill without a second anywhere under heaven.
It was a skill that even Lu Xiaofeng had never seen before.
Ximen Chuixue's eyes shone the brighter. At the sight of an art new and strange he was like a child before a strange new toy, filled with an excitement and delight past describing.
He waited until Su Shaoying had spent one-and-twenty strokes, and only then did his own sword go out.
For he had seen the flaw in the swordplay, one flaw, perhaps, and only one; but one flaw was enough.
His sword-light flashed once, and had run Su Shaoying through the throat.
Blood was on the point again. Ximen Chuixue blew on it, lightly, and the blood ran off the point in drops.

He gazed at the blade's edge, and something desolate and forlorn seemed to come into his eyes; then he sighed, a long sigh, and said, "Why must a youth like you be always in such haste to die? In twenty years, where would you have had me look for such an adversary?"
Such words in another man's mouth would have struck some hearer as mawkish and absurd; but out of his they seemed to carry a bleakness and a killing gravity past all telling.
Hua Manlou said suddenly, "If that's so, why need you have killed him at all?"
Ximen Chuixue's face darkened. "Because the only swordplay I know is the swordplay that kills," he said coldly.
Hua Manlou could only sigh, for he knew the man spoke no lie. Every stroke this man made was a killing stroke, that left neither mercy nor any road back.
"Either you die, or I die." Once his sword thrust out, it left no man any room to choose; not even himself.
A wind came in from beyond the pavilion, still carrying the clean scent of lotus leaves; but it could not carry off the reek of blood within.
Ximen Chuixue turned suddenly and faced Yan Tieshan. "While you do not flee, I do not strike," he said coldly. "Move once, and you die."
Yan Tieshan actually smiled. "Why should I flee? I've no notion what any of you are about."
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. "You ought to know very well."
"But I do not," said Yan Tieshan.
"And Yan Liben?" said Lu Xiaofeng. "Doesn't he know either?"

The corner of Yan Tieshan's eye began to jump again; over the plump white face came a strange, frightened look, and it seemed of a sudden much older. A long while passed before he sighed, and muttered, "Yan Liben died long ago. Why come seeking him now?"
"It's not we who seek him," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Who, then?" said Yan Tieshan.
"The Great King of the Golden Roc," said Lu Xiaofeng.
At the name, Yan Tieshan's already strange face turned stranger and more dreadful still; the fat body spun of a sudden like a top, and a blaze of glorious pearl-light flashed out across the pavilion.
Amid the shining of the pearls, dozens of thin, keen winds shot out in a sudden downpour, driving each at its mark: at Ximen Chuixue, at Hua Manlou, at Lu Xiaofeng.
And in that instant, out of the pearl-light there flashed a breath of sword-force.

The sword-force was cold as frost, the sword-wind like wind through bamboo; swish, swish, swish, swish, a quick flurry of sound, and sword-force and pearl-light alike were gone in an instant, while dozens of pearls came down out of mid-air, every one of them shaved clean in two.
A fast sword. But by now Yan Tieshan himself was nowhere to be seen.
Lu Xiaofeng was gone too.
Out on the lotus pond beyond the pavilion, shapes seemed to flit; a light touch on a lotus leaf, and up they sprang.
Two shapes there were, but the two seemed stuck together, the man behind like the very shadow of the man in front.
The shapes flickered and were gone; but within the pavilion there rose the wind-rush of a sleeve.
And then, all at once, Yan Tieshan was there again.
Lu Xiaofeng too: of a sudden he was back in his seat, as if he had never once left it.

Yan Tieshan stood where he had stood before, but his body leaned now against the high dais, and he panted without cease; in that brief span he seemed to have aged many years more. He had come into the pavilion a middle-aged man in the full flush of health, his face smooth and soft, without so much as a whisker on it; now any man could see him for what he was, an old man of seventy or eighty. The flesh of his face hung loose, the eyelids drooped slack, the eyes had gone dull and lightless; and gasping, sighing, he said in desolation, "I am old now... old..."
Lu Xiaofeng looked at him, and could not help a sigh of his own. "You're old indeed."
"Why do you use an old man so?" said Yan Tieshan.
"Because this old man once ran up a debt to another," said Lu Xiaofeng, "and however old he grows, he'll have to pay it himself."
Yan Tieshan raised his head suddenly. "What debts I owe I'll pay myself, to be sure," he cried. "But when did I ever owe any man a thing?"
"Perhaps you owe nothing," said Lu Xiaofeng. "But what of Yan Liben?"
Yan Tieshan's face worked again. "True enough, I am Yan Liben," he said harshly, "the Steward Yan who ate men and spat out no bone. But since the day I came here, I..."
His voice broke off short, and the twisted, distorted face grew all at once, miraculously, calm again.
And then every man there saw a spurt of fresh blood burst open on his breast, like a splendid flower bursting into bloom.
Only after the blood had sprayed out could they see the inch of sword-point that stood from his chest.
He bowed his head and looked at the bright length of the point, and seemed astonished, and puzzled.
But he was not yet dead. His chest still rose and fell, as though somewhere a bellows were being worked.
Huo Tianqing's face too had gone iron-grey. He rose sharply. "Whose is this murdering hand?" he demanded.

"Mine!" A voice clear and sweet as a silver bell, a body light as a swallow; someone sprang in suddenly through the window, in a diving-suit of black sharkskin that clung close about her slender, stirring shape, water still running off her. Plainly she had this moment come tumbling up out of the lotus pond and into the pavilion.
Yan Tieshan forced his eyes open, staring at her in astonishment, and with the last of his strength brought out three words: "Who are you?"
She had torn off the hood of the diving-suit, and a cloud of soft dark hair fell loose about her shoulders, setting off the pale beauty of her face.

But her eyes were full of hatred and venom. She glared at Yan Tieshan and said fiercely, "I am Princess Danfeng, daughter of His Majesty the Great King of the Golden Roc, come to settle certain old accounts with you."

Yan Tieshan stared at her; his eyeballs bulged suddenly, his body convulsed once, and then he would never move again. Yet in those eyes, thrust out past the lids, there lingered still a strange and uncanny look, whether of astonishment, or of fury, or of fear, none could tell.
Still he did not fall, for the sword was in his breast yet.
The sword was cold. And the blood had gone cold too.
Princess Danfeng turned slowly away at last, and the hatred and the venom in her face had all become a faint, quiet sorrow.
She would have spoken to Lu Xiaofeng, but of a sudden she heard Ximen Chuixue say coldly, "You use a sword too?"
Princess Danfeng was taken aback, and in the end she nodded.
"From this day on," said Ximen Chuixue, "if you use a sword again, I will have your life."
Princess Danfeng, plainly startled, could not help asking, "Why?"
"A sword is not for killing men from behind," said Ximen Chuixue. "Whoever wounds a man from behind is not fit to hold one."
He swung his hand out suddenly; there was a sharp crack as his own sword-point struck the point of the sword in Yan Tieshan's breast.
Yan Tieshan toppled; the sword was knocked from his chest and fell beyond the pavilion.

Ximen Chuixue was already outside the pavilion. He took up the blood-stained sword, gave it a flick of the wrist, and it broke of a sudden into five or six lengths that fell one by one to the ground. A wind blew by; the night mist had just begun to rise off the lotus pond, and his figure was gone into it.
Huo Tianqing had sat down again, and sat now without a motion, the iron-grey face like an iron-grey mask.

But Lu Xiaofeng knew that no expression is often the most grieving expression of all. He sighed softly. "Yan Tieshan was a traitor to the dynasty of the Golden Roc," he said. "So this was no mere private grudge, and no business for an outsider's hand."
Huo Tianqing nodded slowly. "I understand."
"So you needn't blame yourself," said Lu Xiaofeng.
Huo Tianqing was silent a long while. Then he raised his head suddenly. "But it was I who invited you here."
"You did," said Lu Xiaofeng.
"Had you not come," said Huo Tianqing, "Yan Tieshan wouldn't be dead now, at least."
"Your meaning is..." said Lu Xiaofeng.

"I mean nothing else by it," said Huo Tianqing coldly, "than that I'd like to try that lightness-skill of yours, Lu Xiaofeng of the Twin Painted Wings, and that one secret art of yours, the hearts that beat as one through a single thread."
Lu Xiaofeng smiled wryly. "You're set on forcing me to cross hands with you?"
"I am," said Huo Tianqing.
Lu Xiaofeng sighed. But Princess Danfeng had already spun about and come rushing over. "Why must you challenge him?" she cried. "It was me you should've challenged."
"You?" said Huo Tianqing.

Princess Danfeng sneered. "It was I who killed Yan Tieshan, killed him from behind. Try me, if you like, and see whether killing from behind is the only skill I've got." She had just swallowed a bellyful of anger from Ximen Chuixue with nowhere to vent it, and now she turned it on Huo Tianqing.
Huo Tianqing looked at her. "What Yan Tieshan owed you," he said slowly, "I'll repay in his stead. So you may go now."
"You daren't cross hands with me?" said Princess Danfeng.
"Not that I daren't," said Huo Tianqing. "That I won't."
"Why?" said Princess Danfeng.
"Because you're no match for me whatever," said Huo Tianqing mildly.
Princess Danfeng's face flushed red with anger; and suddenly she thrust out ten slender jade fingers and went for Huo Tianqing's eyes with the move called Poison-Dragon Plucks the Pearl.
Her fingers were soft as spring shallots, but the move she used was a savage and a scalding one, and her hand was very fast.

Without a stir of his shoulders or a lift of his legs, Huo Tianqing was of a sudden seven chi away, and had caught up Yan Tieshan's body. "Lu Xiaofeng," he called, "at sunrise I'll wait for you at the Green Wind Temple." The words were not finished before he was beyond the pavilion.
Princess Danfeng bit her lip and stamped her foot, so angry the tears seemed on the very point of falling.
But Lu Xiaofeng smiled at her, of a sudden. "Had you loosed your Flying Phoenix Needles, perhaps he'd not have got away."
"Flying Phoenix Needles?" said Princess Danfeng. "What Flying Phoenix Needles?"
"Your own secret hidden weapon," said Lu Xiaofeng. "The Flying Phoenix Needles."
Princess Danfeng stared at him, then sneered suddenly. "So it seems I not only kill from behind, I kill with hidden weapons too!"
"A hidden weapon's a weapon like another," said Lu Xiaofeng. "Many an honourable man of the martial world carries one."
"But I've never used one," said Princess Danfeng. "I've never so much as heard those three words, Flying Phoenix Needles."
The answer did not surprise Lu Xiaofeng; he had asked only to prove whether that little goblin had been lying yet again.
But Princess Danfeng's very eye-rims had reddened. She bit her lip. "I know you're angry with me," she said, "and say these things on purpose to fix a slander on me."
"And why should I be angry with you?" said Lu Xiaofeng.

"Because you think I should never have come," said Princess Danfeng, "and still less have killed Yan Tieshan." She looked deeply wronged; the shine of tears welled up in her eyes again, and she said with bitterness, "Because you'll never know how cruelly he ruined our house. Had he not betrayed his faith and his duty, we might've had our chance to take back the kingdom and avenge it; but now... now..."
The words were not out before her tears, held back no longer, hung in a string of pearls all down her face.
Lu Xiaofeng could say nothing more.
Who says tears are not a woman's most telling weapon? And with a beautiful woman, the tear-drops are more precious by far than any pearl.
